In the context of my thesis I develop JSDM models on Nimble.

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm trying to build a Nimble model for count-based time-series that contain autocorrelation. Essentially, it's supposed to look like this:

y_t ~ Pois(lambda_t)
lambda_t <- lambda_t-1 * exp(eta + B0 + XB)
eta ~ N(0,sd_eta)
B ~ multivariateN(0,sd_beta)

y_t = count at time t
lambda_t = process mean at t
lambda_t-1 = process mean at t-1
eta = stochastic shock
X = covariate matrix
B0 = intercept

My primary interest is in estimating B0 and B so I can compare models with different sets of covariates. I use the attached scripts in R to generate simulated time-series and the relevant Nimble code. Just run pois_data.R and then nimble_pois.R to reproduce what I'm seeing.

I've only just started learning state-space modelling, Bayes, and MCMC. So, I'm not sure if the model is impossible to estimate accurately or if there's something I could be doing differently with the MCMC to reach convergence. I have had some luck with convergence when using strong priors on B0 and eta, but long MCMC runs (1000000 iterations) still eventually go for a random walk. Any suggestions would be greatly appreciated!

Chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the query.  When I ran your data simulation code,  simdata_counts turned out to be all zeros.  This seems to have created a pathological case for parameter estimation.  The posteriors are to a first glance reasonably mixed, but the B0 values are very negative and some of the other dimensions are sampling a huge range (maybe essentially their priors).  When I add up the terms in the exponent that appears for lambda[j] to get a posterior sample of that exponent for each time step, I get largely very negative values.  So it seems that the posterior is saying there is essentially no information in the data except that lambdas should be zero because the Ys are all zero.  I presume you'll want to try things out with more interesting simulated data, or let me know if I've done something wrong.

A couple of other notes on your model:

Having lambda0 follow a gamma that is mixed over uniform parameters might be excessive.

The random effects eta[j] ("process noise") typically have a std. deviation that is a parameter to be estimated, not fixed at something large.  As written, it's like saying you are sure that extrinsic bumps to the system are of enormous scale rather than estimating the scale of their distribution.

Finally, making eta[j] follow a normal and then inserting it into the deterministic node for lambda[j] creates an inefficient graph.  It means that if eta[j] is sampled in the MCMC, then  *all* of lambda[j]...lambda[T] and the Poisson log probabilities of Y[j]...Y[T] must be calculated, either to accept/reject and/or to update the state of the model.  As T gets big, this does not scale well.

If instead you write

for(j in 2:T) {
loglambda[j] ~ dnorm(loglambda[j-1] + B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]), sd = 1000) ## except that "1000" should be a parameter as noted above, but I just wrote it as you had in your code.
}
for(j in 1:T) {
Y[j] ~ dpois(exp(loglambda[j]))
}

then you will have a more efficient graph.  There is no eta[j], but loglambda[j] is stochastic.  If loglambda[j] is sampled in the MCMC, only the log probabilities of loglambda[j], loglambda[j+1] and Y[j] must be calculated.

Perry

messages.subject_clean: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Nathan, thanks for your interest in NIMBLE.  Let me explain how runMCMC(), and NIMBLE's MCMC samplers in general, operate.

For runMCMC(), you specify the arguments niter, and nburnin.  The default values are niter = 10,000 (total MCMC iterations to run), and burnin = 0 (by default no, burnin iterations are discarded).

The "adaptation" of most of NIMBLE's MCMC samplers operate using continuously decaying adaptation, not any finite adaptation period.  That is, they are "adapting" throughout the entire course of the MCMC, however the magnitude of the adaptation necessarily decays during the MCMC run.  So at first, the tuning parameters adapt a lot, then gradually less and less so.  In the extreme case, after say millions and millions of MCMC iterations, the adaptation (although present) would be negligible.

So, when you specify a burnin of, say nburnin = 1,000, the first 1,000 iterations will be discarded, and runMCMC() will return 9,000 MCMC samples.  For those samples returned, the samplers are still adapting, but much less so than in the initial 1,000 iterations that were discarded.  The default adaptation interval for most samplers is 200 iterations, so this would be discarding the first 5 (and most extreme) adaptive phases.

Does this make sense?  Does it answer your question?

Cheers,
Daniel
NIMBLE development team

I'm not able to reproduce the error that you got with the first model (Myoutput1.txt), but here's something that may help.  When you build a nimbleModel, you can tell NIMBLE the dimensions of the variables in the model by using the "dimensions" argument.  Most of the time, NIMBLE can figure out the dimensions of model variables itself, but for your model, the dimensions of the "b1" variable should be provided in the call to nimbleModel.  In your R script, this would look like:

ord<- nimbleModel(code = ordcode, name = "ord",
                               inits=ordInits,
                               constants = ordconst,
                               data = orddata,
                               dimensions = list(b1 = c(2, 32)))

NIMBLE has difficulty automatically detecting the dimensions of 'b1' because two different sets of dimensions are used in the model code ( "b1[1,1:m[1]]" and "b1[2,1:m[2]]"), so NIMBLE needs to be told explicitly what the correct dimensions of b1 are.  Giving these dimensions may fix the first error you got.

I also have an idea about the strange warnings you're seeing in your second set of output.  I noticed that your model has discrete valued parameters (the I1  and I2 parameters in your initial model).   The MCEM algorithm attempts to find optimal values for all of the stochastic variables in your model that aren't included in the "latentNodes" argument.  So, in your model, the MCEM algorithm is trying to optimize the I1 and I2 variables.  However, the MCEM algorithm uses an optimizer that is not designed to handle discrete parameters, so it ends up proposing non-integer values for these parameters, for example I1 = 0.5.  In turn, this is causing other model calculations to behave incorrectly, since it doesn't make sense for I1 to be anything other than 0 or 1.  To solve this, I think that you might want to include these two variables (I1 and I2) as latent variables in your MCEM algorithm - then they will no longer be optimized.

Hopefully these two suggestions will get the algorithm running for your model.  Please let me know if this doesn't work or if you encounter any other issues though! Thanks,

Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I see several thing going on.

Perhaps most importantly, you have not included samplers for the lambda[j]s.  You can add 'lambda' to the nodes argument to configureMCMC.  Alternatively, I typically omit the nodes argument, which means all non-data stochastic nodes will be sampled, which means I won't forget something by accident.  If you want to customize samplers (as it looks like you do), you can then remove samplers for 'a' and 'b' (poisTSModel_conf$removeSamplers(c('a','b'); poisTSModel_conf$printSamplers() to inspect what you have) before adding the new sampler(s).

It looks like you've accidentally placed a highly informative prior on B0.  I think you want
B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
Without the "sd = ", it will treat 1000 as a precision, so sd = 0.01, effectively assuming B0 must be nearly 0.

It looks like your use of dmnorm is not quite what you want.  The way to interpret the entries in Table 5.2 of the user manual is that you could use either

B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], cholesky=cholA[1:K,1:K], prec_param = 1)
or
B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=A[1:K,1:K]) ## don't need cholA in this case; nimble will calculate it as a "lifted node"

Your code says that cholA is the precision matrix, which I don't think is what you want.

I'm still not sure you have much information on the impact of X is in the simulated time-series.  When I compared a Poisson-normal mixture using the std.dev <http://std.dev>. of 0.001 to the simulated Y values, it looked fairly consistent.  And I see that the B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]) values in the simulation are all very small.  So the Poisson observation error might somewhat swamp the signal in this case, and the estimates might essentially say there are no interesting dynamics, but you'll have to see once you have the model fixed.  It is not uncommon in state-space models to have a hard time separating process noise from observation error for a particular time series.

I don't know the domain context of your model.  It looks like the kind of model people use for population dynamics, where lambda[j] is a latent population density and the lambda dynamics are multiplicative because that's how populations change.  In that case, people typically add process noise on a log scale (i.e., in the exponent) to represent "environmental stochasticity".  If reproduction is high (or mortality is low) due to random conditions in one year, those rates affect the whole population, which corresponds to a random variation on the log scale.  If you add noise on the non-log scale, but with standard deviation that does not vary with time (as you have done in the current code), then effectively you are saying that process noise has a smaller relative impact when lambda is large and a larger relative impact when lambda is small.  That may not correspond to the concepts the model should represent.

If results still don't seem to make sense, you might try providing initial values for the lambda.  In some cases this can be very helpful.  For example, you could set initial lambda to equal Y plus some jitter (or log(Y) + jitter for loglambda, if you switch to the log scale).

Perry

I'm glad to hear things are coming together.

To avoid the inefficient graph, you need to have the latent states themselves be stochastic, so that there is conditional independence through the time-series or latent states.  The loglambda version I suggested previously would do that.  I think the modification from your latest code would be:

for (j in 2:T){
      mu[j] <- inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K])
      loglambda[j] ~ dnorm( loglambda[j-1] + mu[j], sd = stdev)
      lambda[j] <- exp(loglambda[j])
   }

Now loglambda[j] depends on loglambda[j-1] but is conditionally independent from loglambda[j-2] etc.

The model is mathematically equivalent to your code, but the latent states themselves rather than the process noises are written as stochastic.

Perry

messages.body_plain:
> What did we do in NIMBLE 0.6-6 that broke your code?
>
> Chris

Thanks Chris

It turned out that there were just two small issues.

First, the handling of defaults within each sampler. In past versions, we had things like this in the setup code of each sampler
        adaptive       <- control$adaptive
        adaptScaleOnly <- control$adaptScaleOnly
        adaptInterval  <- control$adaptInterval
        scale          <- control$scale
        propCov        <- control$propCov
and now we need things like
        logScale      <- if(!is.null(control$log))           control$log           else FALSE
        reflective    <- if(!is.null(control$reflective))    control$reflective    else FALSE
        adaptive      <- if(!is.null(control$adaptive))      control$adaptive      else TRUE
        adaptInterval <- if(!is.null(control$adaptInterval)) control$adaptInterval else 200
        scale         <- if(!is.null(control$scale))         control$scale         else 1

Second, the way the limits are handled in the reflective sampler. We used to have this
        if(reflective) {
            while(propValue < range[1] | propValue > range[2]) {
                if(propValue < range[1]) propValue <- 2*range[1] - propValue
                if(propValue > range[2]) propValue <- 2*range[2] - propValue
            }
        }
and now we need this
        if(reflective) {
            lower <- model$getBound(target, 'lower')
            upper <- model$getBound(target, 'upper')
            while(propValue < lower | propValue > upper) {
                if(propValue < lower) propValue <- 2*lower - propValue
                if(propValue > upper) propValue <- 2*upper - propValue
            }
        }

With those fixes in place the code works fine on 0.6-6

NIMBLE does end up using sometimes surprisingly large amounts of memory in the steps of building and compiling models and MCMCs.  Some of the issue has to do with R. messages.subject: Re: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
messages.subject_clean: Adaptive phase using runMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Nice question! There are Bayesian purists out there who are very against leaving adaptation on. My impression is that the main issue is a risk of non-stationarity in variance estimates and for this diagnostics tools can provide useful checks.

Inside runMCMC is a loop over your nchains that contains the line
> mcmc$run(niter, progressBar = progressBar)
That means that the buildMCMC runtime parameter reset is taking on the default TRUE value for each chain, so the iteration counter used to slow down adaptation is being reset for each sampler.

Currently many of the samplers have an adaptive flag that can be set in the setup code. You could reset the value of this flag for each sampler in R with something like
> Rmcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$adaptive <- FALSE
but the equivelent in C
> Cmcmc$samplerFunctions[[1]]$adaptive <- FALSE
does not seem to work, so you'd have to recompile - at which point you loose any adaptations obtained from previous MCMC runs.

To be able to toggle adaptation on/off within compiled C code would probably require that an adaptive run time argument is added to buildMCMC and that each sampler has a method function that can be called by buildMCMC's run code to toggle the sampler's adaptive arguments. Perhaps one for the To Do list?

Best
David

messages.body_plain:
Now the temporal dynamics of lambda are a non-stationary random walk.  That can often cause problems in estimation and may not be what you really want.  In this case, the intercept (B[1]) and all of the lambda[j]s are all very highly correlated with each other.  Try cor(samples) and make some pairwise plots to see that.  They seem to be nearly non-identifiable.  A small increase in B[1] can be compensated by the same small decrease in all lambda[j]s, which leaves the probabilities unchanged except for lambda[1].  That means B[1] cannot practically be separated from the lambda[j]s in much of a meaningful way.  It's common to make the dynamics of the (log of the) latent state auto-regressive and anticipate estimates of the auto-correlation between -1 and 1, but only you can say if that makes sense for your problem.

Also your data simulations are extremely variable.  If I run it several times, I sometimes get count series with explosions over many orders of magnitude, and sometimes just mild fluctuations.

Chris,

I'm not able to reproduce the painful memory use you are reporting.

I am encountering a different issue, which is that configureMCMC violates R's limit on recursion depth because of the (non-conditionally independent) format of the model.  Daniel, if you are reading this, perhaps we should impose a fairly small limit of recursion depth during conjugacy checking and simply punt on conjugacy if that is violated?  Chris, please try "useConjugacy = FALSE" in your call to configureMCMC and see if that helps.

It is also worth updating to the current development version of nimble and see if that helps.  To so do, use

library(devtools)
install_github("nimble-dev/nimble", ref = "devel", subdir = "packages/nimble")

(There are a few extraneous diagnostic messages that you may see while running from this version.)

At some points during development we have found large transient memory allocations during model setup due to vectorized calculations in R that exploded in size for some kinds of large models.  We fixed those by reducing how those steps were done.  I don't think any of those changes were recent enough to explain what you are encountering, but it is conceivable.

Finally, if you write your model in the way we've discussed on other threads, making lambda[j] or loglambda[j] stochastic, that should reduce memory usage.  I don't think the reduction will be enough to account for the problem you are reporting, but I am not sure.  The reduction will occur because the graph dependencies will not grow into the hundreds for lambda[j] for large j.  Also the model should run faster for the same reason.

Perry

I don't see high correlations between B[1] and the lambdas, only high correlations between (among) the lambdas. The random walk for lambdas is intentional but I was thinking about adding an autoregression coefficient anyway, so I'll let you know if that helps. The modelling process is ongoing and I'm glad to see the latest challenge might be with the model itself instead of something I did wrong with the mcmc or nimble code---progress!

I think the crazy fluctuations in the simulated data are caused by the random walk covariates (and of course the relevant regression coefficients). Sometimes the system shoots off. The covariates in our real data are not pure random walks and they vary only over some relatively small space, so when I've been testing the nimble model I just rerun the data simulation a couple of times until I get something that looks plausible. When I run the data simulation with 0 for the regression coefficients, the system looks consistent across runs and reflects just the intercept and lambda random walk over a small space and short time (because I'm only looking at dozens of time steps at once---longer series would presumably tend to shoot off like a random walk again eventually because of lambdas dynamics). All of that is to say, I'm just being lazy with the covariates and I think it's responsible for the behavior you're seeing, rather than something related to the dynamics of lambda, at least over short times and for small standard deviations of N(lambda,stdev). If I'm wrong here, please let me know.

I might be willing to deal with non-identifiability in B[1] since the other parameters are converging to the correct estimates every time I've tried. So far, with simulated data, it seems to have no substantial effect, at least on the location of the other B's, though it might be increasing the variance. Anyhow, if none of this involves the MCMC or nimble and it's all about the model itself, I don't expect you to spend any time thinking about it---though I appreciate any thoughts you have!

C

messages.body_plain:
Often people put in a correlation coefficient rather than assuming it is 1, which is what makes it non-stationary.

On Fri, Oct 13, 2017 at 3:55 PM, Chris Carleton <w.cca...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Just checked again and I'm definitely seeing the correlations now. No idea how to solve it. We'll have to think about whether the correlations/non-identifiability is going to be a problem for us. The model needs to contain autocorrelation to be useful in our case. Thanks again, Perry!
>
> C
>
> On Friday, October 13, 2017 at 1:48:57 PM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
> > Good luck with the modeling and let us know any further nimble problems.

> > On Fri, Oct 13, 2017 at 1:41 PM, Chris Carleton <w.cca...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Perry,
> > >
> > > Thanks for the response.
> > >
> > > I don't see high correlations between B[1] and the lambdas, only high correlations between (among) the lambdas. I just looked at a Cor(samples)[B[1],lambdas] and saw only low correlations (near zero, centered on zero overall). So, maybe it's something that only happens for specific simulated data. Did I do something wrong there? I would expect the correlations to be low because B[1] is a constant while lambdas vary as a random walk.
> > >
> > > The random walk for lambdas is intentional but I was thinking about adding an autoregression coefficient anyway, so I'll let you know if that helps. The modelling process is ongoing and I'm glad to see the latest challenge might be with the model itself instead of something I did wrong with the mcmc or nimble code---progress!
> > >
> > > I think the crazy fluctuations in the simulated data are caused by the random walk covariates (and of course the relevant regression coefficients). Sometimes the system shoots off. The covariates in our real data are not pure random walks and they vary only over some relatively small space, so when I've been testing the nimble model I just rerun the data simulation a couple of times until I get something that looks plausible. When I run the data simulation with 0 for the regression coefficients, the system looks consistent across runs and reflects just the intercept and lambda random walk over a small space and short time (because I'm only looking at dozens of time steps at once---longer series would presumably tend to shoot off like a random walk again eventually because of lambdas dynamics). All of that is to say, I'm just being lazy with the covariates and I think it's responsible for the behavior you're seeing, rather than something related to the dynamics of lambda, at least over short times and for small standard deviations of N(lambda,stdev). If I'm wrong here, please let me know.
> > >
> > > I might be willing to deal with non-identifiability in B[1] since the other parameters are converging to the correct estimates every time I've tried. It's also turned out to be the case that the mcmc does converge for B[1] on my real data but the variance is huge. It would be nice to have a "base rate" estimate since that would be scientifically interesting, but our primary interest is in identifying the other B parameters and comparing different models involving different combinations of covariates. So, as long as the model is partially identifiable in terms of the other B's, that's the most important part. So, my major concern will be whether non-identifiability in B[1] is going to significantly affect the reliability of the other B's. So far, with simulated data, it seems to have no substantial effect, at least on the location of the other B's, though it might be increasing the variance. Anyhow, if none of this involves the MCMC or nimble and it's all about the model itself, I don't expect you to spend any time thinking about it---though I appreciate any thoughts you have!
> > >
> > > C

> > >
> > >
> > > On Oct 13, 2017 11:48 AM, "Perry de Valpine" <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > > > Now the temporal dynamics of lambda are a non-stationary random walk.  That can often cause problems in estimation and may not be what you really want.  In this case, the intercept (B[1]) and all of the lambda[j]s are all very highly correlated with each other.  Try cor(samples) and make some pairwise plots to see that.  They seem to be nearly non-identifiable.  A small increase in B[1] can be compensated by the same small decrease in all lambda[j]s, which leaves the probabilities unchanged except for lambda[1].  That means B[1] cannot practically be separated from the lambda[j]s in much of a meaningful way.  It's common to make the dynamics of the (log of the) latent state auto-regressive and anticipate estimates of the auto-correlation between -1 and 1, but only you can say if that makes sense for your problem.
> > > >
> > > > Also your data simulations are extremely variable.  If I run it several times, I sometimes get count series with explosions over many orders of magnitude, and sometimes just mild fluctuations.

> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > for (j in 2:T){
> > > > > > >       mu[j] <- inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K])
> > > > > > >       loglambda[j] ~ dnorm( loglambda[j-1] + mu[j], sd = stdev)

> > > > > > > > > Hi Chris,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I see several thing going on.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Perhaps most importantly, you have not included samplers for the lambda[j]s.  You can add 'lambda' to the nodes argument to configureMCMC.  Alternatively, I typically omit the nodes argument, which means all non-data stochastic nodes will be sampled, which means I won't forget something by accident.  If you want to customize samplers (as it looks like you do), you can then remove samplers for 'a' and 'b' (poisTSModel_conf$removeSamplers(c('a','b'); poisTSModel_conf$printSamplers() to inspect what you have) before adding the new sampler(s).
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > It looks like you've accidentally placed a highly informative prior on B0.  I think you want
> > > > > > > > > B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
> > > > > > > > > Without the "sd = ", it will treat 1000 as a precision, so sd = 0.01, effectively assuming B0 must be nearly 0.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > It looks like your use of dmnorm is not quite what you want.  The way to interpret the entries in Table 5.2 of the user manual is that you could use either
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], cholesky=cholA[1:K,1:K], prec_param = 1)
> > > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > > B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=A[1:K,1:K]) ## don't need cholA in this case; nimble will calculate it as a "lifted node"
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Your code says that cholA is the precision matrix, which I don't think is what you want.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I'm still not sure you have much information on the impact of X is in the simulated time-series.  When I compared a Poisson-normal mixture using the std.dev <http://std.dev>. of 0.001 to the simulated Y values, it looked fairly consistent.  And I see that the B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]) values in the simulation are all very small.  So the Poisson observation error might somewhat swamp the signal in this case, and the estimates might essentially say there are no interesting dynamics, but you'll have to see once you have the model fixed. > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I don't know the domain context of your model.  It looks like the kind of model people use for population dynamics, where lambda[j] is a latent population density and the lambda dynamics are multiplicative because that's how populations change. If reproduction is high (or mortality is low) due to random conditions in one year, those rates affect the whole population, which corresponds to a random variation on the log scale.  If you add noise on the non-log scale, but with standard deviation that does not vary with time (as you have done in the current code), then effectively you are saying that process noise has a smaller relative impact when lambda is large and a larger relative impact when lambda is small.  That may not correspond to the concepts the model should represent.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > If results still don't seem to make sense, you might try providing initial values for the lambda.  In some cases this can be very helpful.  For example, you could set initial lambda to equal Y plus some jitter (or log(Y) + jitter for loglambda, if you switch to the log scale).

> > > > > Now the temporal dynamics of lambda are a non-stationary random walk.  That can often cause problems in estimation and may not be what you really want.  In this case, the intercept (B[1]) and all of the lambda[j]s are all very highly correlated with each other.  Try cor(samples) and make some pairwise plots to see that. That means B[1] cannot practically be separated from the lambda[j]s in much of a meaningful way. The loglambda version I suggested previously would do that.  I think the modification from your latest code would be:
> > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > for (j in 2:T){
> > > > > > > >       mu[j] <- inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K])
> > > > > > > >       loglambda[j] ~ dnorm( loglambda[j-1] + mu[j], sd = stdev)

> > > > > > > > On Tue, Oct 10, 2017 at 9:04 AM, Chris Carleton <w.cca...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > > > > > Hi Perry,
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > Thank again, that's all very helpful!
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I did forget to include lambda—working too long and too late, I guess.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I made the adjustments accordingly and it looks like it's all working now, at least in the few runs I've tried so far. It also appears to be giving sensible results with real data.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I was, at one point, trying to estimate the scale of the error, but switched to a fixed value while troubleshooting in an attempt to limit the potential sources of problems. I've added it back in as you suggested and, like I said, it's working.
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > I'd like to try adding a separate process noise term back in (this is what I was doing with the eta term in the exponential before), but I thought it was responsible for the inefficient graph. Do you have any code I could look at to see how the noise is usually added?
> > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > In case anyone is interested, I've added the scripts of the so-far-functioning model and simulated data.

> > > > > > > > > On Friday, October 6, 2017 at 9:50:55 AM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
> > > > > > > > > > Hi Chris,
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I see several thing going on.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Perhaps most importantly, you have not included samplers for the lambda[j]s.  You can add 'lambda' to the nodes argument to configureMCMC.  Alternatively, I typically omit the nodes argument, which means all non-data stochastic nodes will be sampled, which means I won't forget something by accident.  If you want to customize samplers (as it looks like you do), you can then remove samplers for 'a' and 'b' (poisTSModel_conf$removeSamplers(c('a','b'); poisTSModel_conf$printSamplers() to inspect what you have) before adding the new sampler(s).
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > It looks like you've accidentally placed a highly informative prior on B0.  I think you want
> > > > > > > > > > B0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1000)
> > > > > > > > > > Without the "sd = ", it will treat 1000 as a precision, so sd = 0.01, effectively assuming B0 must be nearly 0.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > It looks like your use of dmnorm is not quite what you want.  The way to interpret the entries in Table 5.2 of the user manual is that you could use either
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], cholesky=cholA[1:K,1:K], prec_param = 1)
> > > > > > > > > > or
> > > > > > > > > > B[1:K] ~ dmnorm(mean=multimu[1:K], prec=A[1:K,1:K]) ## don't need cholA in this case; nimble will calculate it as a "lifted node"
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > Your code says that cholA is the precision matrix, which I don't think is what you want.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I'm still not sure you have much information on the impact of X is in the simulated time-series.  When I compared a Poisson-normal mixture using the std.dev <http://std.dev>. of 0.001 to the simulated Y values, it looked fairly consistent.  And I see that the B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]) values in the simulation are all very small.  So the Poisson observation error might somewhat swamp the signal in this case, and the estimates might essentially say there are no interesting dynamics, but you'll have to see once you have the model fixed.  It is not uncommon in state-space models to have a hard time separating process noise from observation error for a particular time series.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > I don't know the domain context of your model.  It looks like the kind of model people use for population dynamics, where lambda[j] is a latent population density and the lambda dynamics are multiplicative because that's how populations change.  In that case, people typically add process noise on a log scale (i.e., in the exponent) to represent "environmental stochasticity".  If reproduction is high (or mortality is low) due to random conditions in one year, those rates affect the whole population, which corresponds to a random variation on the log scale.  If you add noise on the non-log scale, but with standard deviation that does not vary with time (as you have done in the current code), then effectively you are saying that process noise has a smaller relative impact when lambda is large and a larger relative impact when lambda is small.  That may not correspond to the concepts the model should represent.
> > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > If results still don't seem to make sense, you might try providing initial values for the lambda.  In some cases this can be very helpful.  For example, you could set initial lambda to equal Y plus some jitter (or log(Y) + jitter for loglambda, if you switch to the log scale).

> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Thanks for the query.  When I ran your data simulation code,  simdata_counts turned out to be all zeros.  This seems to have created a pathological case for parameter estimation.  The posteriors are to a first glance reasonably mixed, but the B0 values are very negative and some of the other dimensions are sampling a huge range (maybe essentially their priors).  When I add up the terms in the exponent that appears for lambda[j] to get a posterior sample of that exponent for each time step, I get largely very negative values.  So it seems that the posterior is saying there is essentially no information in the data except that lambdas should be zero because the Ys are all zero.  I presume you'll want to try things out with more interesting simulated data, or let me know if I've done something wrong.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > A couple of other notes on your model:
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Having lambda0 follow a gamma that is mixed over uniform parameters might be excessive.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > The random effects eta[j] ("process noise") typically have a std. deviation that is a parameter to be estimated, not fixed at something large.  As written, it's like saying you are sure that extrinsic bumps to the system are of enormous scale rather than estimating the scale of their distribution.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > Finally, making eta[j] follow a normal and then inserting it into the deterministic node for lambda[j] creates an inefficient graph.  It means that if eta[j] is sampled in the MCMC, then  *all* of lambda[j]...lambda[T] and the Poisson log probabilities of Y[j]...Y[T] must be calculated, either to accept/reject and/or to update the state of the model.  As T gets big, this does not scale well.
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > If instead you write
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > for(j in 2:T) {
> > > > > > > > > > > > loglambda[j] ~ dnorm(loglambda[j-1] + B0 + inprod(X[j,1:K], B[1:K]), sd = 1000) ## except that "1000" should be a parameter as noted above, but I just wrote it as you had in your code.
> > > > > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > > > > for(j in 1:T) {
> > > > > > > > > > > > Y[j] ~ dpois(exp(loglambda[j]))
> > > > > > > > > > > > }
> > > > > > > > > > > >
> > > > > > > > > > > > then you will have a more efficient graph.  There is no eta[j], but loglambda[j] is stochastic.  If loglambda[j] is sampled in the MCMC, only the log probabilities of loglambda[j], loglambda[j+1] and Y[j] must be calculated.

> > > > > > > > > > > > Perry

Hi Giovanni,

The problem is that we take anything that is a 'constant' and plug in the actual numerical values in the model. So 'var0' (and also 'mn0') no longer exist in the model as variables once this substitution happens. This is fine when 'Ind' is also provided as constants but in your case NIMBLE is trying to use a dynamic index to index a constant, which won't work. We overlooked this possibility and hence don't provide a useful error message here.

All you need to do is the following. First, provide 'var0' and 'mn0' via 'inits', so that we treat 'var0' and 'mn0' as variables in the model. Second, we need some help here with the dimensions since there is no easy way for us to know that mn0 and var0 are vectors of length 10 (this is because we don't require initial values for model variables when a model is created and because mu0 and var0 are not created via a deterministic or stochastic assignment). The use of the 'dimensions' argument allows NIMBLE to know what size these two variables are.

logChi2Model <- nimbleModel(logChi2Code, constants = list(n = n, w0 = w0), # , mn0 = mn0, var0 = var0),
                            data = list(y = y), inits = list(var0 = var0, mn0 = mn0, Ind = rep(5, n)),
                            dimensions = list(mn0 = 10, var0 = 10))

-Chris

Hi All,

When Nimble calculates the WAIC for a given mcmc/model, how does it determine what parameters to sample if the observations are not totally independent?

In my case, I've built a structural time-series model and each observation is dependent on the previous one AND the various latent parameters in the model. I was thinking about altering the WAIC to account for that temporal structure, but then I started wondering how Nimble calculates the WAIC. If it uses the relationships in the graph of the model to determine what needs to be sampled as a parameter, then I'm wondering whether it's already including the previous observation in the parameter vector for the posterior prediction. If so, then I might not need to do anything differently and I could maybe argue that Nimble has dealt with the dependence for me. If not, and Nimble only uses the strictly latent nodes as parameters for WAIC, then I'll probably have to think more carefully about my adjustment to WAIC and write my own function to estimate it given the mcmc posterior samples.

Any thought here would be greatly appreciated.

Chris

(Forgot to post this to nimble-users!)

Hi Chris,

Here's a little bit more detail on NIMBLE's WAIC procedure:

1)  The WAIC algorithm iterates over the posterior samples that have been obtained by the MCMC algorithm.  For each set of posterior samples, these sampled posterior values are inserted into the model.  To see which parameters are being inserted into the model, you can check the column names of as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples).

2)  For each of these posterior samples that have been inserted into the model, new values for every stochastic, non-data node that depends on these sampled nodes are then simulated conditional upon the set of posterior values that have been inserted into the model.

3)  The probabilities for each of the data nodes in the model are then calculated, conditioned upon the posterior values of the nodes sampled by the mcmc algorithm and the simulated values of any other stochastic downstream nodes.

These three steps repeat for each of the posterior samples that were obtained by the MCMC, and then the WAIC is calculated using all of the data node probabilities obtained in step 3.

I'm not sure if this will make anything clearer, but here's an example using a simple time series model:

sigmaX ~ dunif(0, 10)  ##  sigmaX is an unknown parameter
x[1] ~ dnorm(0, sigmaX)
y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], 1)
for(t in 2:T){
  x[t] ~ dnorm(x[t-1], sigmaX)  ## x[t] is a latent state at time t, depends on x[t-1]
  y[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], 1)  ## y[t] is the observed data at time t
}

If we run an MCMC on the above model and get posterior samples for sigmaX, then the WAIC algorithm will proceed by, for each posterior sample for sigmaX:

- simulating data values for x[1], ... x[T] given that posterior value of sigmaX
- calculating probabilities p( y[t] | x[t] ) for t = 1, ... T, given the newly simulated x[t] values

I'm not totally sure whether this description gives an answer to your question or not - if not, or if you have any other questions, definitely let me know and I'd be happy to think more carefully about the problem.  Additionally, if you do decide to code your own WAIC function, the source code for NIMBLE's WAIC calculation can be found here (starting on line 147):

https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_build.R

Possibly looking at that code could help when you're writing a customized WAIC.

Thanks!

Nick
